newsitem.title: FRANCE: French court weighs limits on English on Internet.
newsitem.headline: French court weighs limits on English on Internet.

text.p: A Paris court faces the ticklish question Monday of deciding whether French laws aimed at promoting the French language and culture can reach into cyberspace.

The court is to hold a hearing on a legal challenge by two private French groups against a site on the global Internet computer network set up by the French campus of the Georgia Institute of Technology and written entirely in English.
Officials of Georgia Tech Lorraine say the Internet site is in English because all its courses are taught in English and all its students are required to be fluent in English.
But the campus in Metz, eastern France, happens to be in a country that has for years waged an uphill battle against the Anglo-Saxon domination of cyberspace.
Experts in the largely uncharted field of cyberspace law are looking to the Georgia Tech Lorraine case for clues to the future course of cyberspace regulation around the world.
The complaint against Georgia Tech Lorraine was filed by two private associations, Defence of the French Language and Future of the French Language.

The Paris-based groups say they fear for the future of French culture in an English-dominated world and see the Internet as simply the latest Anglo-Saxon menace to their national language and traditions.
The Georgia Tech Lorraine site, whose Internet address is www.georgiatech-metz.fr, offers course descriptions, a guide to the campus and other information useful to current and potential students.
It also provides access to Internet pages put together by some of the 29 students listed on the site.
Francois Malassenet, deputy director of Georgia Tech Lorraine and a Frenchman, said the school had nothing against French and had no interest in debating the wisdom of its laws.

"We have students of all nationalities, but to be admitted to the Georgia Institute of Technology you must speak English. Since English is a requirement, we do not see the need to offer the information in French as well."
He said the school had been flooded with electronic messages in recent days backing its stand.
"I think those who do not support us could be counted on the fingers of half a hand," he said.
